ch08.anchor: the eighth year before the Republic
ch08.note: Chinese sources here reckon years from the founding of the Republic in 1912 (its Year 1). Dates are counted forward as 'the Nth year of the Republic' (民国, so Republic 23 = 1934) and backward as 'the Nth year before the Republic' (民前); 'the eighth year before the Republic' is 1904. Quoted documents in this book keep such dating; the running narration has been converted to Western years.
The li (里), the standard Chinese unit of distance, is about half a kilometer (roughly a third of a mile), so sixty-odd li is some thirty kilometers. It recurs throughout for road and march distances.

ch08.anchor: a great gated mansion of four courtyards
ch08.note: A siheyuan (四合院), the classic northern Chinese dwelling: single-story halls ranged on four sides of an enclosed courtyard, entered through one gate. A compound of several courtyards in depth, as here, marks a large and wealthy household.

Anti-Bolshevik Russians who fled the 1917 Revolution and the ensuing civil war, many of them ending up stateless in the cities of North China—Harbin, Tianjin, Shanghai—where they worked as guards, musicians, tutors, and hired hands. 'White' here means counter-revolutionary, opposed to the Bolshevik 'Reds.'

ch08.anchor: the cart ahead is a warning to the cart behind
ch08.note: The proverb qian che zhi jian (前车之鉴), 'the overturned cart ahead is a lesson to the one behind'—learn caution from the disaster that befell those who went first.

From the saying 'when the city gate catches fire, the woe reaches the fish in the moat' (城门失火，殃及池鱼): to put out the blaze the moat is drained, and the fish die—bystanders ruined by a calamity that was none of their doing.

ch08.anchor: every bush and tree a soldier
ch08.note: The idiom cao mu jie bing (草木皆兵), from the rout of Fu Jian at the Fei River in 383: his army in panic mistook the grass and trees on the hills for enemy troops—to be so gripped by fear that one sees threats everywhere.

Tianjin's old full name, Tianjinwei (天津卫): a wei was a Ming-dynasty military garrison, and the city grew from the garrison post established here in the early fifteenth century to guard the river approach to Beijing.

ch08.anchor: a man should make himself strong
ch08.note: An echo of the Book of Changes: 'As Heaven moves ever with strength, so the noble man never ceases to strengthen himself' (天行健，君子以自强不息)—the classic Chinese ideal of tireless self-reliance and self-improvement.
